metaDescription: Six wall-mounted electric patio heaters compared on wattage, weather rating, remote and timer controls, and installation for a clutter-free patio.
introParagraphs: A wall-mounted patio heater keeps the floor clear and aims warmth straight at your seating. Most use infrared carbon tubes that warm people and objects directly instead of heating the air, which is why they hold up better in a light breeze than a fan heater would. They also run silently and need no fuel, only an outlet or a wired connection.

We evaluated six distinct wall-mount models based on product specs and buyer feedback, merging repeat listings of the same heater into one pick. The details that separated them were wattage and whether the unit plugs in or must be hard wired, the weather rating on the listing, how it is controlled, and how much hardware you get for mounting.

Mounting height, wiring and outlet capacity all change real results more than a headline wattage figure. The buying criteria below explain how to read those numbers, and the choose sections map common situations to a named pick.

products.name: hykolity 1500W Infrared Wall Mount Heater, 35.5 in
products.description:
The hykolity is a 35.5 in wall-mount heater with a 1500W infrared system and dual carbon tubes. The maker says it delivers warmth in about a second, and the two-tube layout spreads heat from top to bottom of the unit. A remote control and a timer that runs up to 24 hours cover everyday control.

The listing makes a point of safety and weather sealing. It is ETL-certified, with three layers of protection including tip-over shutoff and an overheat safety cutoff. An IP55 rating means the housing is dust protected and resists water jets, and the aluminum housing is described as corrosion-resistant, which suits an uncovered patio.

At 1500W it matches the blessny, the Danluke and the sundate on power, so the decision rests on controls and certification, and the ETL listing is the clearest differentiator. It is less powerful than the 3000W DR-239 and ThermoMate, but it avoids the extra wiring those require. For most patios with an outlet nearby, it is the most balanced pick.
products.bestFor: Most patios that want a certified, weather-sealed 1500W heater with remote control.
pros: ETL-certified with three layers of protection
IP55 housing resists dust and water jets
Dual carbon tubes spread warmth top to bottom
Remote and 24H timer for easy control
cons: Only 1500W, so coverage is limited for large patios
Mounting height and spacing need planning

products.name: DR. INFRARED HEATER DR-239 3000W Wall or Ceiling Heater
products.description:
The DR-239 is a 3000W carbon infrared heater rated at 10,260 BTU, which is double the wattage of the 1500W picks. The listing says it delivers instant, clean heat with no waiting, and it is rated IP55 for indoor and outdoor use, so it suits patios, garages and workshops alike.

It ships with both wall and ceiling mounting brackets, so you can pick whichever surface suits your layout, and a remote lets you switch between power levels. The higher output makes it the strongest choice for a big patio or for people who sit farther from the unit.

The trade-off is electrical. A 3000W heater draws far more current than a 1500W unit, so check the listing for the voltage and confirm with an electrician that your circuit can support it. Compared with the ThermoMate, which is explicitly hard wired at 240V, the DR-239 is the better candidate if you want a high-wattage unit with simple brackets. Against the hykolity at 1500W, it gives double the power but demands more from your installation.
products.bestFor: Larger patios and workshops that need high output and a choice of wall or ceiling mounting.
pros: 3000W (10,260 BTU) is the strongest in the lineup
Both wall and ceiling brackets are included
IP55 weatherproof for indoor and outdoor use
Remote switches between power levels
cons: High wattage demands a capable circuit
Overkill for a small seating area

products.name: ThermoMate Infrared Patio Heater 3000W 240V Hard Wired
products.description:
The ThermoMate is a 3000W carbon fiber infrared heater that runs on 240V and is hard wired. The maker says it heats in about three seconds and covers about 100 sq. ft. outdoors or 130 sq. ft. in an enclosed space. A remote switches between a 1500W low setting and a 3000W high setting and sets a timer up to 24 hours.

Because it is hard wired, it does not plug into a wall outlet, so installation is not a casual afternoon job. That is the main trade-off, and a licensed electrician should handle it. The reward is dependable high output with no extension cord, which suits a permanent patio setup.

Compared with the DR-239, which also offers 3000W, the ThermoMate is the better pick when you want a clear coverage figure and a deliberate low and high mode. Compared with the 1500W models, it covers a notably larger area. It is not the best pick for renters or anyone who might move, because the wiring stays when you leave.
products.bestFor: Permanent installations on larger patios where an electrician can wire a 240V circuit.
pros: 3000W with stated 100 sq. ft. outdoor coverage
Switches between 1500W and 3000W modes
24H timer and remote control
No cord to trip over or route
cons: Not suitable for renters or temporary setups

products.name: blessny 1500W Wall Mounted Electric Heater
products.description:
The blessny is a 1500W infrared wall heater with a carbon fiber tube and an oxidized sprayed aluminum shell. The maker says it produces heat in about three seconds. A 6.0 ft cable and wall-mount hardware are included, and the listing mentions clear instructions.

Its best feature is the IP65 rating, one step above the IP55 of the hykolity. IP65 means the housing is fully dust tight and resists water jets, which is the stronger rating for a patio that sees rain or hose spray. The unit is run with a remote and a 24-hour timer, and the listing claims silent operation.

The 6.0 ft cable is practical but limits placement: the heater must be mounted within reach of an outlet, so plan the height and cable path ahead of time. At 1500W it is on par with the Danluke and the sundate. Against the hykolity, it gains a stronger water rating but does not list the same ETL certification, so safety-minded buyers should compare those two closely.
products.bestFor: Exposed patios where rain, dust or hose spray are a concern.
pros: IP65 rating resists dust and water jets
Includes wall-mount hardware and a 6.0 ft cable
Carbon fiber tube heats in about three seconds
24H timer with remote
cons: Listing does not mention ETL certification
6.0 ft cable limits placement near an outlet

products.name: Danluke 1500W Wall Mounted Electric Patio Heater
products.description:
The Danluke is a compact 1500W wall heater using a carbon fiber element for focused warmth. It measures about 25.59 x 5.16 x 2.36 in, which is shorter than the hykolity at 35.5 in, so it fits tighter wall spaces. The maker describes the design as space saving.

Control comes from both a remote and a touch panel on the unit. Having both is handy: the remote works from your seat, and the panel works if the remote goes missing. The listing does not state a weather rating or a timer in the portion we reviewed, so check the full page before relying on it in heavy rain.

The shorter body means a narrower heating footprint than the 35.5 in hykolity, so it suits a pair of chairs rather than a long bench. It is a sensible choice for a small porch or a covered corner. Against the sundate, which also offers touch and remote control, the Danluke is the simpler listing, but it gives you fewer confirmed extras.
products.bestFor: Small porches and tight wall spaces where a slim 1500W heater is enough.
pros: Compact size fits narrow wall sections
Remote and touch panel both included
Carbon fiber element gives focused warmth
Space-saving, floor-free design
cons: Listing gives no clear weather rating
Narrower heat spread than longer units

products.name: sundate Wall-Mounted Electric Patio Heater, 1500W
products.description:
The sundate is a 1500W radiant wall heater with three heat levels and a carbon fiber tube. Heat is targeted, and the maker describes it as instant. You can control it from a touch panel on the unit or with the remote, and a 24-hour timer is included.

A waterproof design is listed for rain and moisture, along with dual safety protection, though the portion we reviewed does not give an IP number. That makes it harder to compare directly with the hykolity at IP55 or the blessny at IP65, so read the full listing to confirm the rating.

Three heat levels let you run it lower on mild evenings, which saves electricity and avoids over-heating a small seating spot. In practice, it is closest to the hykolity in feature set, with a similar timer and remote. If you want easy dual controls and a familiar layout, it is a dependable pick, but the lack of a stated IP rating is the main caveat.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want three heat levels with both touch and remote control.
pros: Three heat levels for mild or cold evenings
Touch panel and remote both included
24H timer for automatic shutoff
Dual safety protection listed
cons: No IP rating stated on the listing

buyingCriteria.explanation: Wattage sets both heat and the electrical load. A 1500W heater like the hykolity or the blessny is sized for a standard household outlet, while the 3000W DR-239 and ThermoMate draw roughly double the current. The ThermoMate is hard wired at 240V, so it needs an electrician and a dedicated circuit. Check your outlet and breaker capacity before choosing a high-wattage unit.

An IP rating tells you how well the housing resists dust and water. IP55 on the hykolity and DR-239 resists dust and water jets, and IP65 on the blessny is fully dust tight with the same water jet resistance. A higher second digit means stronger water protection, but rain-rated is not submersion-proof. For an exposed patio, favor IP55 or better, and check that the listing actually states a number, as the Danluke and sundate listings we reviewed do not.

Infrared heaters work best when mounted high enough to cover the seating without overheating anyone and far enough from walls and combustibles. Each maker lists its own minimum distances, and the manual governs. The ThermoMate lists a recommended minimum mounting height, and its coverage figures assume correct placement. Measure your wall and seating before you buy.

A remote and timer turn a wall heater from a chore into a convenience. The hykolity, blessny, ThermoMate and sundate list 24-hour timers, and the Danluke and sundate add touch panels on the unit. A timer helps you avoid leaving the heater on overnight. Pick a remote with clear, large buttons if hand dexterity matters to you.

Look for a recognized certification mark and automatic protections. The hykolity is ETL-certified and lists tip-over shutoff and an overheat cutoff. Overheat protection appears on several listings, but certification varies, so do not assume it. Safety features matter most in homes with children, pets or flammable awnings nearby.

A longer heater like the 35.5 in hykolity spreads warmth wider than the 25.59 in Danluke. The ThermoMate states 100 sq. ft. outdoors and 130 sq. ft. enclosed, which is the clearest coverage claim in the group. Treat all coverage numbers as rough, because wind, mounting height and distance change what you feel. A 1500W unit suits one seating cluster, not a whole deck.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power and installation
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared wattage and how each unit is installed, based on product specs and buyer feedback. The ThermoMate and the DR-239 lead on output at 3000W, while the 1500W picks are simpler to install. The ThermoMate's hard-wired 240V design was credited for output but marked down for installation effort.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weather resistance
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the stated IP ratings and housing materials. The blessny at IP65 leads on paper, followed by the hykolity and the DR-239 at IP55. Where a listing did not give a number, as with the Danluke and sundate, we scored cautiously.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls and convenience
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at remotes, timers and touch panels. The sundate and Danluke offer both touch and remote, while the hykolity, blessny and ThermoMate pair a remote with a 24-hour timer. Ease of use for seniors depends on button clarity, which varies by remote.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted certifications and automatic protections. The hykolity stands out with ETL certification, tip-over shutoff and an overheat cutoff. Other picks list overheat or dual protection without naming a certifying body.

howWeEvaluated.title: Coverage and fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed physical size and stated coverage. The ThermoMate gives the clearest coverage numbers, the DR-239 offers the most output with flexible mounting, and the Danluke is the most compact. In the lineup, the hykolity balances size, safety and weather rating best.

cards.label: Plug-in 1500W
cards.text: A plug-in heater uses a cord and a standard outlet, so installation is a bracket and a few screws. The hykolity, blessny, Danluke and sundate fall on this side. The blessny includes a 6.0 ft cable, so mount it close to an outlet.

cards.text: A hard-wired heater connects directly to the circuit, so there is no cord and no outlet limit. The ThermoMate is explicitly hard wired at 240V and needs an electrician. Choose plug-in for flexibility and renters, hard wired for permanent, high-output setups.

faq.q: Which wall-mounted patio heater is best overall?
faq.a: The hykolity 1500W is the most balanced pick. It combines ETL certification, an IP55 housing, dual carbon tubes, a remote and a 24-hour timer. If your patio is large and you can have a circuit wired, the 3000W ThermoMate gives more output.

For the 1500W plug-in models, usually not, as long as the outlet can carry the load. The ThermoMate is hard wired at 240V and needs a licensed electrician. For the 3000W DR-239, check the listing voltage and have your circuit confirmed.

faq.q: How high should I mount it?
faq.a: Follow the minimum mounting height in the manual for your model, because each maker sets its own. Mounting too low can overheat guests, and mounting too high reduces the warmth you feel. Measure your seating height and wall space before drilling.

faq.q: Does IP65 mean it is better than IP55?
faq.a: It means stronger dust sealing, because IP65 is fully dust tight while IP55 is dust protected. Both resist water jets. For most covered patios, either is adequate, but for an open deck the blessny's IP65 offers a bit more margin.

faq.q: Can I leave it on all night?
faq.a: Avoid it. Use the 24-hour timer or a shorter run, and turn the heater off when you leave. Infrared units are not designed as unattended overnight heaters.

faq.q: Will a 1500W heater warm a whole patio?
faq.a: No. A 1500W infrared heater warms the people and objects in front of it, so it suits one seating group. For wider coverage, consider the 3000W ThermoMate or DR-239, or use more than one heater.

faq.q: How do I maintain a wall-mounted heater?
faq.a: Switch it off and let it cool, then wipe the housing with a damp cloth and check the cord and bracket occasionally. Do not spray water directly into vents. Re-check mounting screws each season.
